2023 · NeurIPS · Benchmarks & Evals

TaskBench: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Task Automation

A benchmark that scores LLMs on the whole task-automation pipeline at once — decomposing an instruction into steps, choosing the right tools, and filling in their arguments — built by sampling structured "tool graphs" and having an LLM invert them into instructions, so the test set scales without an army of human annotators.

// the gap

What problem is this solving?

LLM-based "task automation" — turning a user instruction like "convert this video to anime style, dub it, then post it to TikTok" into a working sequence of tool calls — is the load-bearing skill behind agent systems such as HuggingGPT, AutoGPT, and TaskMatrix.AI. But by late 2023 there was no single benchmark that tested the whole pipeline. The authors group task automation into three stages — task decomposition (breaking the instruction into sub-tasks), tool selection (choosing which tools to call and how they depend on each other), and parameter prediction (filling in each tool's arguments) — and argue existing benchmarks each cover only a slice of this. APIBench and ToolBench build tasks from API documentation with template-based sampling, which limits logical consistency; MetaTool focuses narrowly on the binary decision of whether to use a tool and which one, without modeling dependencies between tools; ToolQA emphasizes question-answering correctness in a fixed domain; ToolAlpaca relies on self-instruct-style generation, while API-Bank generates from API documentation and then leans heavily on human verification to control quality — both approaches cap scale and dependency complexity.

Two deeper gaps recur across these predecessors. First, dependency modeling: real multi-tool tasks have resource dependencies (tool A's output type must match tool B's expected input) and temporal dependencies (tool A must run before tool B), and none of the compared benchmarks represent this structure explicitly — Table 1 of the paper marks "Tool Dependency" as absent (✗) for APIBench, ToolBench, MetaTool, and API-Bank alike, versus present (✓) for TaskBench. Second, data-generation scalability: Table 1 shows every compared benchmark leans on human verification for quality control (APIBench, MetaTool, and ToolBench all list "Human Verification"; API-Bank lists "Auto-generation + Human Verification"), and the authors' own diagnosis is that this reliance on manual verification and template-based generation — not any single benchmark's raw sample count — is the bottleneck: prior benchmarks "rely heavily on human verification or simple template-based generation, potentially limiting their scalability and diversity" (Related Works, p.4). Table 1's scale row bears this out unevenly rather than as a clean ranking: samples range from APIBench's 2,365 up to MetaTool's 21,127, and API-Bank's 6,135 is reported in a different unit (interactions, not samples) that isn't directly comparable to the rest.

// how it works

The method

TaskBench's central abstraction is the Tool Graph (TG): a graph G = (T, D) where T is a set of tools and D is a set of dependency edges between them. Two tools are connected if either a resource dependency holds (tool a's input type matches tool b's output type) or a temporal dependency holds (tool a must execute after tool b). The benchmark builds three such tool graphs across three domains: Hugging Face Tools (23 AI-task tools such as Image-to-Text or Text-to-Image, connected by resource dependencies, 225 edges), Multimedia Tools (40 more user-facing tools like file downloaders and video editors, 449 edges), and Daily Life APIs (40 tools such as web search and shopping, connected mostly by temporal order, 1,560 edges).

Data generation follows a three-step Back-Instruct data engine (Figure 2). First, a sub-graph is sampled from the full tool graph in one of three structural modes — Node (a single standalone tool call), Chain (a sequential pipeline), or DAG (a directed acyclic graph where a tool can depend on multiple predecessors or feed multiple successors) — with subgraph size drawn from {1,…,10} tools and mode ratio fixed at Node:Chain:DAG = 3:7:8. Second, GPT-4 is prompted to invert the sampled subgraph into a natural user instruction (BackInstruct1(Gs) → I) — this is the trick that lets the dataset scale: rather than writing instructions and then figuring out what tools they need, the tool dependencies are fixed first and an LLM back-generates a plausible instruction that would require exactly that combination. Third, given the generated instruction, GPT-4 fills in each tool's parameters and produces the final task-decomposition steps and tool invocation graph (BackInstruct2(Gs, I) → {P, Ḡ}).

Quality control has two layers. A self-critic mechanism — both an LLM-based critic (checks semantic alignment between generated data and the sampled subgraph) and a rule-based critic (checks that the generated graph's nodes/edges structurally match the sampled subgraph) — filters candidates before human review. Then human verification confirms logical consistency, following a calibration session where reviewers scored sample naturalness, complexity, and alignment together. After both filters, the appendix reports final verified sample counts of 7,546 (61.76% of 12,217 generated) for Hugging Face Tools, 5,584 (62.71% of 8,904) for Multimedia Tools, and 4,320 (60.42% of 7,150) for Daily Life APIs.

Evaluation runs as TaskEval, three metric families matched to the three pipeline stages: task decomposition is scored with Rouge-1/Rouge-2/Rouge-L against the ground-truth step text; tool selection is scored with Node-F1 (n-F1, does the predicted tool set match) and Edge-F1 (e-F1, do predicted dependency edges match) plus Normalized Edit Distance (NED) for chain structures; parameter prediction is scored with Parameter-Name F1 (t-F1) and Parameter-Name-and-Value F1 (v-F1). The three domains and three evaluation stages combine into a single evaluation harness that a model runs through end to end.

// what they found

The results

Across all three stages and all three domains, GPT-4 is the most consistent performer, though not uniformly dominant. On tool selection (Table 3), GPT-4's overall Node-F1/Edge-F1 on Hugging Face Tools is 81.54/54.70, on Multimedia Tools 90.90/69.27, and on Daily Life APIs 96.91/80.53 — the highest overall Edge-F1 in every domain among the ten LLMs in the paper's main tool-selection table, Table 3 (GPT-4, Gemini-Pro, Claude-2, GPT-3.5-Turbo, text-davinci-003, Mistral-7B-v0.3, CodeLlama-13B, Nous-Hermes-13B, Vicuna-13B-v1.5, and Llama-2-13B-Chat). Appendix A.7 extends the same three-stage evaluation to a wider roster — 17 models for task decomposition (Table 12) and 18 for tool selection (Table 13), adding models like WizardLM-13B, Baichuan-13B-Chat, CodeLlama-7B, Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Vicuna-7B-v1.5, Llama-2-7B-Chat, InternLM-Chat-7B, and (tool selection only) LongChat-7B-v1.5 — and GPT-4's Edge-F1 lead holds across that larger set too. Edge prediction is consistently harder than node prediction — the paper reports roughly a 20-percentage-point gap between node-F1 and edge-F1 scores across models, meaning models are considerably better at guessing which tools are needed than at getting their dependency wiring right.

On parameter prediction (Table 4), GPT-4 again leads with overall v-F1 of 60.86 (Hugging Face Tools), 72.31 (Multimedia Tools), and 71.14 (Daily Life APIs), while open-source models trail noticeably — e.g. CodeLlama-13B's overall v-F1 is 18.87 on Hugging Face Tools versus GPT-4's 60.86. On task decomposition (Table 12), GPT-4 posts Rouge-L of 47.21 / 56.22 / 82.16 across the three domains respectively, and the paper's own analysis notes it runs roughly 10 points higher in R1/R2 than the next tier of models. One domain-specific surprise: CodeLlama-13B is the strongest model at Daily Life APIs task decomposition, scoring R1 89.86 / R2 83.27 / RL 86.12 — even ahead of GPT-4's 85.07/72.36/82.16 on that domain — which the authors attribute to code-centric pretraining helping structure sequential API calls.

The benchmark's own construction quality is separately validated: a human evaluation of 50 anonymized samples rated Back-Instruct's Naturalness/Complexity/Alignment/Overall at 3.89/4.01/3.66/3.85 (out of 5), clearly ahead of a Self-Instruct baseline (2.18/2.01/3.64/2.61) and a Back-Instruct-without-edges ablation (3.44/3.27/3.62/3.44) — evidence that encoding tool dependencies in the sampled subgraph, not just tool names, is what drives more natural and complex generated instructions. Separately, TASKEVAL's automated rankings of models correlate strongly with human judgment: average Kendall's τ = 0.89 and Spearman's ρ = 0.78 across the three domains (Table 9).

// does it hold up?

The eval read

TaskBench's core methodological move — generating tool-dependency graphs first, then back-translating them into instructions with an LLM — is genuinely clever for scaling structured data, but it also means the entire benchmark's ground truth — the gold subgraphs every model's output is deterministically matched against — is GPT-4-generated and GPT-4-self-critiqued structure, which raises the usual self-preference concerns in a benchmark that also evaluates GPT-4 as a top performer. The authors' own error analysis is admirably transparent about the resulting noise: of 148 randomly sampled TaskBench instances, 18 (nearly 12%) were flagged as erroneous by human labelers, breaking down as Incorrect Tool Dependency 29.4%, Mismatched Parameter Types 23.5%, Impractical Instructions 17.6%, Incorrect Parameter Value 17.6%, and Incomplete Instructions 11.8% (Figure 3). A ~12% label-error rate is nontrivial for a benchmark whose edge-level metrics already separate models by single-digit F1 points — a chunk of that gap could be measuring dataset noise rather than model capability.

baselines

The main-table roster (GPT-4, Gemini-Pro, Claude-2, GPT-3.5-Turbo, text-davinci-003, Mistral-7B-v0.3, CodeLlama-13B, Nous-Hermes-13B, Vicuna-13B-v1.5, Llama-2-13B-Chat) was reasonably current for late 2023 and spans proprietary/open-source and general/code-specialized models, which is exactly the right axis to probe (the CodeLlama result on Daily Life APIs shows it). The appendix (Tables 12-14) widens this to 17-18 models and does add an 8B Llama-3-Instruct — but it lands near the bottom of the field everywhere (e.g. 9.27 overall n-F1 / 2.64 e-F1 on Hugging Face Tools tool selection, versus GPT-4's 81.54/54.70), which reads less like "Llama 3 is weak at this" and more like an under-tuned prompt/parsing setup for a small instruct checkpoint the authors otherwise treat as a footnote. Either way, the roster is now dated — no GPT-4o/4-turbo, no larger Llama-3 variants, no function-calling-native models (which is precisely the capability being tested), and no comparison against purpose-built function-calling fine-tunes. A benchmark whose headline claim is "reflects capability in task automation" needs refreshing against models actually trained for tool use, not just prompted.

contamination

Because every instruction and gold graph is synthesized on the fly by GPT-4 from sampled subgraphs (not scraped from any public corpus), classic train/test leakage from web-crawled pretraining data is unlikely in the way it is for, say, MMLU. The more relevant risk is a different kind of contamination baked into the reference labels themselves, not into how they're graded: TaskEval's scoring is fully deterministic string/graph matching against the gold subgraph (Rouge-1/2/L for decomposition; n-F1, e-F1, and NED for tool selection; t-F1 and v-F1 for parameter prediction — Sec. 4.2-4.3) — there is no LLM judge at grading time. But GPT-4 is both the sole author of that gold answer key (via Back-Instruct) and its own construction-time self-critic filter (Sec. 3.2.4), and it is also the strongest model being evaluated. Any GPT-4-specific regularities in how it phrases steps or shapes tool-dependency graphs are therefore baked into the single reference every model — including GPT-4 itself — is deterministically matched against, which could inflate GPT-4's scores (and depress models with different-but-valid phrasing/structuring conventions) independent of true task-automation skill.

what's missed

The metrics (n-F1, e-F1, NED, t-F1, v-F1, Rouge) are all structural/lexical matches against a single gold graph, but real task automation often has multiple valid tool-invocation paths to the same outcome (e.g., a different but equally correct ordering, or a substitute tool with the same effect) — a rigid gold-graph match would penalize a correct-but-different solution as an error, conflating "wrong" with "differently right." The metrics also don't capture actual execution success (did the plan, if run, actually accomplish the user's request?) since TaskBench never executes the tools — it only checks whether predicted graphs/parameters match reference ones on paper.

would raise confidence

Three things: (1) a contamination-independent human/execution-based sanity check on a stratified sample from the current leaderboard, verifying the F1 gaps reflect real capability differences rather than the ~12% baseline noise rate; (2) an ablation swapping the data-generation model away from GPT-4 (e.g., using a different frontier model or an ensemble) to test whether the benchmark still ranks models the same way; (3) an updated leaderboard with 2024-2025 tool-use-native models, since the current comparison set is now two model generations behind the frontier.

// bottom line

TaskBench's Tool Graph + Back-Instruct idea is a real methodological contribution — it is the first of this benchmark family to make dependency structure a first-class, scalably-generated part of the test set rather than an afterthought — and its 0.89 Kendall's τ against human judgment is solid validation. But the benchmark inherits its blind spots from its own generator: a GPT-4-authored answer key that every model is deterministically string/graph-matched against, with an admitted ~12% error rate, evaluated on a model lineup that is now over two years stale. Treat its rankings as directionally right about relative task-automation strength circa 2023, not as a precise, contamination-free measuring stick for today's models.

// takeaways

What to remember

  1. TaskBench is the first benchmark to test task decomposition, tool selection, and parameter prediction together as one pipeline, using an explicit Tool Graph to model resource and temporal dependencies between tools — something APIBench, ToolBench, MetaTool, and API-Bank each lack (Table 1).
  2. Its data engine, Back-Instruct, samples a tool subgraph (Node/Chain/DAG, ratio 3:7:8) first and has GPT-4 invert it into an instruction — a scalable alternative to template- or API-doc-based generation that human raters preferred (Naturalness/Complexity/Alignment/Overall 3.89/4.01/3.66/3.85 vs. Self-Instruct's 2.18/2.01/3.64/2.61).
  3. GPT-4 leads across most metrics but not universally — CodeLlama-13B beats it on Daily Life APIs task decomposition (R1 89.86 vs. 85.07), and edge/dependency prediction is uniformly harder than node/tool-selection prediction by roughly 20 F1 points across every model tested.
  4. The benchmark's own audit found ~12% of generated samples contain errors (mostly incorrect tool dependencies, 29.4% of errors), a caveat worth weighing against any fine-grained model ranking drawn from it, and the evaluated model roster (GPT-4, Gemini-Pro, Claude-2, GPT-3.5, text-davinci-003, and several 13B open-source models) is now dated relative to current tool-use-native LLMs.
